entries.topic: Who summoned, attended and ran the Council of Nicaea, 325

claims.text: Constantine's letter to Alexander and Arius (c.324) called the dispute 'of a truly insignificant character' and 'this truly idle question' (VC II.68, 71)

Constantine summoned the bishops and allowed some 'the use of the public means of conveyance' (VC III.6); Eusebius counts bishops that 'exceeded two hundred and fifty' (VC III.8); a Persian and a Scythian bishop attended, one from Spain; the aged bishop of the imperial city was represented by presbyters (VC III.7)
Constantine entered in glittering raiment and sat on 'a low chair of wrought gold' (VC III.10); he assisted 'the argument of each party in turn' (VC III.13)

Council met May to late July 325; Socrates dates opening 20 May; Hosius of Corduba most likely presided; Constantine took part in Greek but did not vote; Rome represented by presbyters Victor (Vitus) and Vincentius; five Western bishops listed (Hosius, Caecilianus of Carthage, Nicasius of Die, Marcus of Calabria, Domnus of Pannonia); reports 250-300, 318 traditional, signature lists 200-220 names; 1,200-1,900 total including presbyters and deacons
Acesius, Novatian bishop, was called to the council by Constantine, accepted the creed and Easter decision, kept his separation; Constantine: 'take a ladder and ascend alone to heaven'
Frumentius consecrated bishop for Aksum by Athanasius traditionally 328 or 340-346, i.e. after Nicaea
Arius c.250-336, Alexandrian priest; Thalia c.323; declared heretic at Nicaea; Arius taught a created, finite Christ
Controversy began 318; Thalia survives only in fragments quoted mainly by opponents (Athanasius, De Synodis)

Socrates I.8, quoting Eusebius's Life of Constantine Book III, gives 'the number of bishops exceeded three hundred' (VC III.8 as transmitted reads 'exceeding two hundred and fifty'); Socrates himself says 318 'recognized and acquiesced' in the creed

entries.topic: Creed, homoousios, exiles, burning of Arius's books, Easter, Melitians, canons

claims.text: Eusebius of Caesarea's letter (Socrates I.8): 'our most pious emperor himself was the first to admit' the creed correct, exhorting all to subscribe, 'with the insertion, however, of that single word homoousios', which the emperor explained as not indicating corporeal affections
Creed of 325: one substance (homoousion) with the Father; anathematises those who say 'there was a time when the Son of God was not'; 20 canons; no scripture list

Socrates I.8 names five who objected to homoousios: Eusebius of Nicomedia, Theognis of Nicaea, Maris of Chalcedon, Theonas of Marmarica, Secundus of Ptolemais; synodal letter: Theonas and Secundus 'suffered the same condemnation'; edict exiled Arius with Eusebius and Theognis, who later tendered a declaration of changed sentiment
Constantine's letter 'to the bishops and people' (Socrates I.9): Arians to be called 'Porphyrians'; any treatise of Arius 'consigned to the flames'; concealment punished by death
Synodal letter: Melitius to remain in his city without authority to ordain; Easter: brethren in the East who kept it 'when the Jews did' to conform to Rome and Alexandria

Canon 6: ancient customs in Egypt, Libya and Pentapolis prevail so Alexandria has authority there, as is customary for Rome; Antioch keeps its privileges. Canon 7: Aelia (Jerusalem) honour saving the metropolis. Canon 8: Cathari (Novatian) clergy received; Canon 19: Paulianists rebaptised; Canon 20: prayer standing on Sundays and Pentecost
Constantine's Easter letter (VC III.18-19) calls Jews a 'detestable Jewish crowd' and 'nation of parricides who slew their Lord'
Nostra Aetate 4 (28 Oct 1965): Christ's passion 'cannot be charged against all the Jews, without distinction, then alive', nor against Jews today; decries antisemitism

Easter: council adopted method independent of the Jewish calendar, did not specify computation; homoousios had been condemned at Antioch 264-268; Eusebius of Caesarea credits Constantine with the term; Constantine and Hosius backed it
Eusebius of Nicomedia signed after opposition; exiled a few months after the council; restored c.329; baptised Constantine 337; bishop of Constantinople 339-341
Arius restored to communion by Synod of Jerusalem 336, died 336 in Constantinople before reception; scholars agree book-burning was enacted to some degree but no executions recorded

Arius: 'there was a time when the Son was not'; Constantine later lenient, recalled exiles; Constantius II encouraged Arians; Rimini-Seleucia 359; Jerome: world 'awoke with a groan to find itself Arian'

Earliest extant uses of homoousios are in 2nd-c. Gnostic writings: Basilides (first half 2nd c., threefold sonship consubstantial with the non-existent God) and the Valentinian Ptolemy's Letter to Flora; Origen first Trinitarian use; semi-Arians objected it was unscriptural; Alexander and Hosius defended it
Theognis of Nicaea eventually signed the Nicene creed with the other Arian supporters, was excommunicated after the council for not denouncing Arius, and was exiled

entries.topic: Myths about Nicaea tested: canon, vote on divinity, burned gospels, reincarnation, Synodicon/Voltaire, creed today

claims.text: Synodicon Vetus (c.887-920): books placed by the altar, prayer that inspired works be found on top; earliest source claiming canon settled at Nicaea; first printed by Johannes Pappus 1601; Voltaire popularised the claim
Voltaire retold the altar story, adding 'It is a pity that this eloquent procedure has not survived'

Dan Brown's Da Vinci Code claimed Christ's divinity passed by 'a relatively close vote'; Hagen (America, 2006) answers that the dispute was discussed since the apostles and the 'close vote' was all but two
Pliny c.111-113: Christians sang 'a hymn to Christ as to a god'
Ignatius of Antioch: 'For our God, Jesus Christ, was... conceived in the womb by Mary' (Eph 18)
Second Council of Constantinople 5 May-2 June 553; 15 anti-Origen canons signed before council formally opened; anathema I against 'the fabulous pre-existence of souls'

381 creed adds Holy Spirit clauses, 'whose kingdom shall have no end', drops anathemas; first attested at Chalcedon 451; Filioque added in Latin churches late 6th c., Roman liturgy 1014; 381 text is the liturgical form
Constantinople 381: Theodosius I, ~150 bishops, no Western attendance, Holy Spirit section; canon 3 gives Constantinople 'the prerogative of honour after the Bishop of Rome'
Paul: 'after fourteen years I went up again to Jerusalem with Barnabas' (Gal 2:1) — the meeting Paul attended was in Jerusalem in the first century

Constantine's edict addressed 'Novatians, Valentinians, Marcionites, Paulians, ye who are called Cataphrygians' (VC III.64); forbade them to 'assemble yourselves together' in public or 'any private house'; 'all the houses of prayer... which belong to heretics' to be 'made over without delay to the catholic Church' (VC III.65)

VC III.66: after the edict, searches were made for the heretics' forbidden books; some feigned conversion, sincere returners were tested and readmitted; Eusebius does not say what was done with the books
